defects.description: Originals and thumbnails share a bucket, but the ObjectCreated trigger has no specified original-only filter or processing guard; thumbnail writes can therefore trigger recursive processing and unexpected charges.

The welcome-email failure path does not distinguish DynamoDB event-source-mapping failure handling from a Lambda asynchronous DLQ. Specify mapping retry/record-age limits and an on-failure destination, or explicitly enqueue failed work.

Welcome-email idempotency is asserted through R18 but has no described enforcement mechanism. DynamoDB stream processing is at least once; define durable deduplication state and handling of ambiguous SES outcomes rather than assuming each subscription record is processed once.
R19 has no concrete upload expiry, object-key scope, or validation path. A signed image Content-Type does not establish that the uploaded bytes are an image.
Issuing a presigned URL is incorrectly represented as a Lambda-to-S3 write; URL generation does not upload an object, although the separate author-to-S3 upload edge is correct.

reviews.summary: The serverless services and PITR/versioning settings fit the request, but thumbnail recursion protection, stream failure handling, and welcome-email deduplication need concrete designs.

defects.description: Recording a subscription and then calling SES creates a dual-write failure window: the subscription can persist without a welcome email, while retries can duplicate a successful send. Idempotent subscriber writes alone do not satisfy R16; add durable dispatch state or an outbox and an explicit deduplication policy.
The presigned-upload connection is drawn as a Lambda-to-S3 write despite its text correctly describing a direct author upload. Draw the client-to-S3 transfer separately from URL creation.
The private bucket needs an explicit CloudFront origin-access policy and prefix-scoped upload permissions. Upload URL expiry and function least-privilege permissions are also unspecified.
No DynamoDB PITR, S3 versioning, or restore approach is selected, leaving accidental deletion and overwrite recovery undefined.

defects.description: R14 names migration and validation but supplies no database/file transfer method, consistency strategy, rehearsal, or cutover/rollback sequence. Select native tooling or services such as DMS and DataSync and define the migration steps needed to support the three-month deadline.

The two application instances have no specified automatic replacement or recovery mechanism. Use a two-AZ Auto Scaling group or equivalent recovery automation, integrate load-balancer health checks, and validate surviving-AZ capacity.

Security-group relationships, database credential storage, instance IAM permissions, and database/NFS transport encryption are unspecified despite the otherwise useful private placement and at-rest encryption.
Private instances have no documented endpoint or egress path for CloudWatch logs, management, and patching; define the required VPC endpoints or resilient outbound connectivity.
Database connections are classified as reads, and NFS connections are classified as reads while explicitly describing reads and writes; use read/write semantics to avoid implying read-only access.

reviews.summary: EC2, Multi-AZ RDS, and regional EFS are appropriate low-change migration choices, with explicit encryption, but migration execution and application-tier self-healing are incomplete.

RDS and EFS at-rest encryption are not selected. Neither can be assumed encrypted across all creation methods; specify encryption and keys before provisioning, especially because existing unencrypted RDS instances cannot simply have encryption enabled in place.

reviews.summary: The target services fit a minimally changed two-AZ migration, but encryption choices, migration execution, and automatic application-instance recovery need to be specified.

preference.why: Both specify DynamoDB PITR and S3 versioning and share the same processing weaknesses; S3 and DynamoDB already provide at-rest encryption by default, so A's added encryption labels do not establish a material advantage for these requirements.

B correctly models the direct client-to-S3 presigned upload, while retaining the same economical serverless topology; both still need reliable welcome-email dispatch, and omitted S3/DynamoDB encryption labels are not themselves a security regression.

A explicitly selects RDS/EFS encryption and identifies an authentication boundary while preserving the same low-change migration topology; both need a concrete migration plan and application-tier recovery automation.
